rows.english: The Sixty Verses on Reasoning say as well, The world is something that ignorance causes; Why? For the Buddhas say it is so. And why then would it be wrong to say That this world is only conceptions. The meaning of this verse, according to the commentary, is that none of the many worlds that exist does so through some essence of its own: none of them are anything more than products of our conception.

rows.english: The Buddha first turned the wheel by teaching the Four Truths of Realization three times through in twelve different aspects. From this teaching on the Four Truths alone, some disciples who belonged to the class of Listeners and whose minds were ripe grasped the meaning of dependent origination, free from the extreme of thinking of things as self-existent. It has been explained by the savior Nagarjuna in his treatises, and by Master Chandrakirti in his work on the Commentary on the Sixty Verses on Reasoning, that the scriptures of the Lower Way even describe explicitly the most subtle form of selflessness on many occasions. The second time the Buddha turned the wheel he taught in great detail about the selflessness of both the person and phenomena as is found in the brief, medium-length and extensive sutras on the Perfection of Wisdom, as well as in other works. The third time he turned the wheel he gave the teaching of the Cycle of No Return which deals extensively with the subject of method.

rows.english: Sarva mangalam! May goodness ever prevail! The Root Text of Arya Nagarjuna's Sixty Verses on Reasoning The Sixty Verses on Reasoning Note that for this final, combined presentation of the root text, we have used the Tengyur version of the Tibetan, as found in the Derge edition. Within Gyaltsab Je's commentary, we have retained his version of the root text, which appears to be a different translation from the Sanskrit. That translation thus has considerable value, as most of these "alternate" translations that were not included into editions of the Tengyur have been lost-and they may especially give great insight into the original Sanskrit, large portions of which are still missing for this text. For consistency, we retain the English translation of the verses from within the commentary. As described in the introduction to this volume, we have relied for the Sanskrit on the edition by Li Xuexu and Ye Shaoyong; see bibliography entry C1. Unfortunately, only portions of the original Sanskrit are still extant. Sections with major manuscript differences, such as the obeisance, are self-evident from a glance at the differing translations recorded here.

rows.english: (verse 60) III. Arya Nagarjuna's dedication of the virtue created by this composition A Topical Listing of the Writings of Arya Nagarjuna We created this listing of the works of Arya Nagarjuna as more of a biographical exercise, than a definitive, bibliographical one. It is based primarily on three versions of the Tengyur, or collections of traditional Tibetan translations of some 3600 classical commentaries from ancient India: the Derge (widely considered the most authoritative); the Sertri ("gold calligraphy," perhaps older); and the Nartang (a solid alternative edition). We did not attempt a close analysis of additional versions of the Tengyur; and it may be that there are a few other authentic works by Arya Nagarjuna to be found there. We have not generally included works by The Arya which are reported but not actually found in these editions of the Tengyur. In some case the attribution of works to Nagarjuna is questioned by the extremely careful & competent compilers of the various Tengyurs; it was a common corruption in ancient times to say something like "my book is so good, it may as well have been written by Nagarjuna"-and then in time the book would actually be credited to him. We have studied these cases in the ancient catalogs, and we agree fully with these compilers' opinions, and have not included those particular titles. We have relied most heavily upon the truly masterful ancient native Tibetan catalog to the Derge edition. The works in the Derge Tengyur have been very admirably listed and analyzed by the creators of the great Tohoku University Catalog of this collection, and we have relied heavily upon their work. We have also availed ourselves of the fine work of Professor Lokesh Chandra in bringing the often corrupt Tibetanized Sanskrit titles into order. The number of folios in the works are patchy in the originals and may be off by one or two pages, but not more-and so they give a good idea of the relative size of each title; although of course with Arya Nagarjuna a work of 20 folios can change the history of a continent for the next 2,000 years. In some cases the same work may be referred to by different names in different editions of the Tengyur; we have tried to avoid listing both titles but a few cases may have snuck in. We have not re-created Sanskrit titles, as we consider this an inexact and potentially misleading exercise; where a title is not mentioned in situ, we have noted that fact. The translations of the titles into English is by the two translators of the present volume. We have broken the titles down into subject categories, according to our judgement and a quick review of the contents of works. In ordering them, we generally follow the lead of the native creators of the Derge Tengyur. These categories may perhaps be polished in time, but for now are very indicative of topics that The Arya considered important; which is the purpose of the exercise for our present volume. rows.acip: ,RIGS PA DRUG CU PA LAS KYANG , 'JIG RTEN MA RIG RKYEN CAN DU, , GANG PHYIR RDZOGS PA'I SANGS RGYAS GSUNGS, , DE YI PHYIR NA 'JIG RTEN 'DI, , RNAM RTOG YIN ZHES CIS MI 'THAD, , CES GSUNGS PA'I DON 'GREL PAR 'JIG RTEN RNAMS RANG GI NGO BOS MA GRUB PA RTOG PAS BTAGS PA TZAM DU BSHAD CING ,
rows.wylie: rigs pa drug cu pa las kyang , 'jig rten ma rig rkyen can du, , gang phyir rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas gsungs, , de yi phyir na 'jig rten 'di, , rnam rtog yin zhes cis mi 'thad, , ces gsungs pa'i don 'grel par 'jig rten rnams rang gi ngo bos ma grub pa rtog pas btags pa tsam du bshad cing
rows.english: The Sixty Verses on Reasoning say as well, The world is something that ignorance causes; Why? For the Buddhas say it is so. And why then would it be wrong to say That this world is only conceptions. The meaning of this verse, according to the commentary, is that none of the many worlds that exist does so through some essence of its own: none of them are anything more than products of our conception.

rows.acip: ,RIGS PA DRUG CU PA LAS KYANG , 'JIG RTEN MA RIG RKYEN CAN DU, , GANG PHYIR RDZOGS PA'I SANGS RGYAS GSUNG , , DE YI PHYIR NA 'JIG RTEN 'DI, , RNAM RTOG YIN ZHES CIS MI 'THAD, , MA RIG 'GAGS PAR GYUR NA NI, , GANG ZHIG 'GAG PAR 'GYUR BA DE, , MI SHES PA LAS KUN BRTAGS PAR, , JI LTA BUR NA GSAL MI 'GYUR, , ZHES GSUNGS TE,
rows.wylie: rigs pa drug cu pa las kyang , 'jig rten ma rig rkyen can du, , gang phyir rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas gsung , , de yi phyir na 'jig rten 'di, , rnam rtog yin zhes cis mi 'thad, , ma rig 'gags par gyur na ni, , gang zhig 'gag par 'gyur ba de, , mi shes pa las kun brtags par, , ji lta bur na gsal mi 'gyur, , zhes gsungs te
rows.english: Now the Sixty Verses on Reasoning says, The world is something that ignorance causes; Why? For the Buddhas say it is so. And why then would it be wrong to say That this world is only conceptions. If one were to end his ignorance, Then how is it that the thing that's ended, Despite our misunderstanding, could never Disappear, even in conceptions?

rows.acip: ,RIGS PA DRUG CU PA LAS KYANG , 'JIG RTEN MA RIG RKYEN CAN DU, , GANG PHYIR RDZOGS PA'I SANGS RGYAS GSUNG , , DE YI PHYIR NA 'JIG RTEN 'DI, , RNAM RTOG YIN ZHES CIS MI 'THAD, , MA RIG 'GAGS PAR GYUR NA NI, , GANG ZHIG 'GAG PAR 'GYUR BA DE, , MI SHES PA LAS KUN BRTAGS PAR, , JI LTA BUR NA GSAL MI 'GYUR, , ZHES GSUNGS TE,
rows.wylie: rigs pa drug cu pa las kyang , 'jig rten ma rig rkyen can du, , gang phyir rdzogs pa'i sangs rgyas gsung , , de yi phyir na 'jig rten 'di, , rnam rtog yin zhes cis mi 'thad, , ma rig 'gags par gyur na ni, , gang zhig 'gag par 'gyur ba de, , mi shes pa las kun brtags par, , ji lta bur na gsal mi 'gyur, , zhes gsungs te
rows.english: Now the Sixty Verses on Reasoning says, The world is something that ignorance causes; Why? For the Buddhas say it is so. And why then would it be wrong to say That this world is only conceptions. If one were to end his ignorance, Then how is it that the thing that's ended, Despite our misunderstanding, could never Disappear, even in conceptions?

rows.acip: DPE MA GRUB STE MAR ME RANG GIS RANG GSAL BAR BYED PA MA YIN TE MAR ME RANG GIS GSAL BAR BYA BA MIN PA'I PHYIR TE RANG GIS RANG GSAL MI DGOS SHING MI NUS PA'I PHYIR RO, ,DE LTA NA MUN PAS KYANG RANG GZHAN GNYIS KA SGRIB PAR BYED PAR 'GYUR NA DE MI RIGS TE GANG GI PHYIR NA MUN PA LA MUN PAS BSGRIBS PA MED PA'I PHYIR RO, , BSGRIBS NA BUM PA GOS KYIS BSGRIBS PA BZHIN DU MUN PA'ANG MI MTHONG BAR 'GYUR RO, , 'DI DAG NI RTZA SHE LAS GSUNGS PA LTAR RGYAS PAR SHES PAR BYA'O,
rows.wylie: dpe ma grub ste mar me rang gis rang gsal bar byed pa ma yin te mar me rang gis gsal bar bya ba min pa'i phyir te rang gis rang gsal mi dgos shing mi nus pa'i phyir ro, ,de lta na mun pas kyang rang gzhan gnyis ka sgrib par byed par 'gyur na de mi rigs te gang gi phyir na mun pa la mun pas bsgribs pa med pa'i phyir ro, , bsgribs na bum pa gos kyis bsgribs pa bzhin du mun pa'ang mi mthong bar 'gyur ro, , 'di dag ni rtsa she las gsungs pa ltar rgyas par shes par bya'o
rows.english: But your example does not hold true. A lamp is not something which illuminates itself, because it is not something which is the object illuminated by it. There is no need for it to illuminate itself, and it could never do so anyway. If it could, then darkness too shroud both itself and other objects. This though could never be, for the reason that there is no such thing as darkness shrouding darkness. If it did shroud darkness, then it would be like shrouding a vase with a piece of cloth, and we would be unable to see the darkness itself. For these points I am enlarging upon statements found in the Root Text on Wisdom [by the realized being Nagarjuna].

rows.english: Just before you start the ritual, recite the following: Pictured as Angel, I disappear, Fade into emptiness, no projections. As quick as a fish flicks on the surface, I see myself once more with one head, two arms; My head's center tip is marked with an om, The throat with an ah, the heart with a hung.
